pages.title: The first assignment
pages.text: Maya woke before sunrise. An overnight storm had damaged Greenford's old bridge, and her editor needed a reporter. Before her first assignment, Maya worked for a news channel. Her editor handed her a microphone and a notebook. 'Check every detail,' he said. Down by the river, a repair team was already busy. The engineers worked on repairs to the bridge. Maya photographed the broken railing. Her first assignment had begun, but she did not yet know whose lives it would change.
pages.predict: What might Maya discover when she reaches the flooded neighbourhood?
pages.observe: Describe the people, objects and actions in these two pictures. How do the people seem to feel? Give a visual clue.

scenes.alt: Maya stands in the newsroom with her microphone and identity badge.
Engineers examine plans and repair the railing of a storm-damaged bridge.

feedback.worked for: Work for names an employer or someone you help. The bridge repairs were the task the engineers were doing, so use work on.

Maya photographed the broken railing. Her first assignment had begun, but she did not yet know whose lives it would change.

pages.title: An unexpected call
pages.text: Across Greenford, television screens showed streets underwater. The families heard about the flooding on the news. Maya watched the bulletin, worried about her friend Elena. She had not received a message from her since the storm. Maya finally heard from Elena when her phone rang. 'I'm safe at the shelter,' Elena said. 'But our elderly neighbour, Mr Reed, hasn't arrived.' Maya felt relief and worry at once. She wrote his name in her notebook and called the rescue coordinator.
pages.predict: What should Maya do with information that has not yet been confirmed?

challenges.success: Hear about means to receive information about an event or topic.

feedback.heard about: Hear about means to receive information about someone or something. Elena called Maya directly, so use hear from.

challenges.success: Hear from means to receive news or a message directly from someone.

'I'm safe at the shelter,' Elena said. 'But our elderly neighbour, Mr Reed, hasn't arrived.' Maya felt relief and worry at once. She wrote his name in her notebook and called the rescue coordinator.

pages.title: A sound in the silence
pages.text: At home, a family sat beside a battery radio. They needed to know which streets were closed. The family listened to the instructions on the radio. Near Mr Reed's house, a firefighter raised one hand. Everyone stopped talking. In complete silence, the firefighter listened for cries for help. Maya waited on the dry lane. An upstairs curtain moved. Was someone there? She held her breath as the firefighter pointed towards the window.
pages.predict: What could the moving curtain mean? Suggest two possibilities.
pages.observe: Describe the people, objects and actions in these two pictures. How do the people seem to feel? Give a visual clue.

A firefighter asks for silence and tries to detect a voice from an upper window.

feedback.listened for: Listen for means to wait and try to detect a sound. The family could already hear the instructions and was paying attention to them, so use listen to.

challenges.success: Listen to means to pay attention to a sound or message.
challenges.sentence: The family listened to the instructions on the radio.

feedback.listened to: Listen to means to pay attention to a sound that is already there. In the silence, the firefighter was trying to detect a possible voice, so use listen for.

challenges.success: Listen for means to wait and try to detect a particular sound.
challenges.sentence: In complete silence, the firefighter listened for cries for help.

Maya waited on the dry lane. An upstairs curtain moved. Was someone there? She held her breath as the firefighter pointed towards the window.

pages.title: The missing neighbour
pages.text: The rescue boat moved slowly between the flooded houses. Mr Reed had not reached the shelter, and nobody knew where he was. The rescuers were looking for the missing neighbour. Back at the command post, two rescuers spread a street map across a table. To choose their route, the rescuers were looking at a map. They found a route around the fallen branches. Then a small light appeared upstairs. Mr Reed was there with his dog! The crew brought them safely to dry ground. Maya finally had a confirmed rescue to report.

pages.title: At the shelter
pages.text: At the shelter, a cold family stood beside a table of supplies. A parent held out her hands to a volunteer. Because they were cold, the family asked for blankets. Mr Reed sat nearby with his dog and a cup of tea. Outside, Maya opened her notebook and began questioning an official. During the interview, Maya asked about the damage. 'Which homes are affected?' she said. She wanted facts, not rumours. The official explained what the crew had checked and what was still unknown.

pages.title: More than a headline
pages.text: By lunchtime, Maya was ready to face the camera. She stood on dry ground beside the rescue boat. During her live broadcast, Maya reported on the flood. She explained how Mr Reed had reached safety. Meanwhile, new volunteers arrived, unsure where they were needed. On arrival, the volunteers reported to the shelter coordinator for instructions. One would organise food; another would prepare beds. Maya realised that behind every headline there were people doing patient, practical work.

feedback.reported on: Report on means to give information about a topic. The volunteers went to their coordinator for instructions, so use report to.

pages.title: The dangerous shortcut
pages.text: Dark clouds returned. On television, a weather presenter pointed to the approaching storm. To alert viewers to the danger, the presenter warned people about the approaching storm. Near the shelter, a pedestrian tried to take a shortcut through a flooded street. A firefighter stopped her at the barrier. The firefighter warned people against walking through floodwater. 'Stay on the dry path,' he said. She turned back. Maya added the warning to her next update: clear information could help someone make a safer decision.
pages.predict: How can a reporter share a warning without making an unverified claim?

pages.title: People who help
pages.text: Inside the shelter, a nurse gently wrapped a bandage around a man's arm. By treating their injuries, the nurse cared for injured people. Nearby, neighbours gathered around Elena's photograph of her damaged home. They discussed how to support her family in the coming weeks. Their concern showed that the neighbours cared about the affected families. Mr Reed's dog slept under a chair. Maya put down her microphone. Her story was about much more than water and broken buildings; it was about people who mattered to one another.

pages.title: A question for the mayor
pages.text: Two days later, some homes still had no clean water. Residents held empty containers beside a dry tap. The frustrated residents complained about the lack of clean water. Elena agreed to speak for them. At the town hall, she placed their written complaint and photographs on the mayor's desk. To present the residents’ grievance, Elena complained to the mayor. The mayor promised an update that afternoon. Maya recorded the promise, knowing that her job was not finished. She would need to check what happened next.

pages.title: A different kind of ending
pages.text: A week later, clean water deliveries had reached the neighbourhood. Maya checked the delivery records before sharing the update. At the community centre, a teacher explained how rivers overflow. During the lesson, the students learned about floods. In another room, emergency planners studied photographs of crowded routes and shelters from the previous evacuation. To improve the next evacuation, the planners learned from past mistakes. Mr Reed arrived with his dog and thanked the rescue crew. Maya closed her notebook. A good report, she now understood, follows the story beyond the headline.
